proposals.name: LaTeX/markup macro leakage
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much unrendered LaTeX or markup syntax (e.g., \textit{}, \emph{}, \url{}, \textsf{}, inline math like $x$, or markdown-style **bold**) appears literally in the text, as opposed to being properly rendered or absent. 0 = no visible markup residue, 10 = pervasive throughout. Do not judge whether this is good or bad, only how much is present.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('\textit{e.g.,}', '\textit{in-domain}') and R34 ('\textsf{S}em\textsf{A}ntic', '\url{...}') contain literal unrendered LaTeX tokens in the abstract body, likely from pasting source text without full cleanup; this is a copy-paste/formatting habit unrelated to the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Coined pronounceable method acronym or brand name
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much does the abstract introduce and repeat a distinctive, pronounceable brand-style name or acronym for its proposed method or artifact (a capitalized short name used repeatedly as the method's identity)? Score the presence and repetition of the branded name, not whether the name is clever or the method is good.
proposals.rationale: R16 repeats the brand names 'CerebroVoice' and 'MoBSE' and R34 repeats the stylized acronym 'SAFARI' multiple times, a naming/marketing habit distinct from R02 or R12, which describe comparably substantive contributions without a repeated branded acronym.

proposals.name: Superlative and novelty-claim adjective density
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how frequently the text uses superlative or novelty-asserting words such as 'novel', 'first', 'state-of-the-art', 'significant(ly)', 'outperforms', 'remarkable'. Count only the density of such words; do not assess whether the claims are true or the work is actually novel.
proposals.rationale: R38 and R48 each use words like 'novel', 'significant', and 'outperforms' multiple times in a short space, versus R02 and R12, which use almost none of this vocabulary while describing comparably substantive contributions.

proposals.name: Explicit self-citation of one specific prior named method
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the abstract names and directly builds on or critiques ONE specific prior named method or paper (e.g., 'building on X (Author, Year)', 'extending the Y method', 'unlike the vanilla Z') as opposed to describing the general problem area without pinning to a single named predecessor. Score only the presence of this specific-predecessor-naming pattern, not whether the critique is well-founded.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's established practice or track record in this exact narrow subfield
proposals.rationale: R36 explicitly cites 'gradual stacking (Reddi et al., 2023)' and R17 builds directly on 'the hybrid latent refinement (HLR) method', both textual signs of an author embedded in a narrow prior lineage; this plausibly correlates with genuine domain expertise but is not itself a quality signal from the text alone.

proposals.name: Large-scale infrastructure or resource-access markers
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the abstract cites large-scale resources -- very large sample sizes or dataset counts, access to proprietary frontier models by name, or costly human-expert evaluation panels -- as evidence of scale, regardless of whether that scale produced better results.
proposals.upstream_parent: author or lab access to compute, proprietary APIs, or funding
proposals.rationale: R52 reports 'data from n > 5000 LLMs' and R09 reports an evaluation with '11 scientists across three criteria'; both signal resource access that could both bias reception and genuinely support more reliable findings, so this channel is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Promise-vs-delivered code or data availability phrasing
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate whether the abstract offers an already-live, dereferenceable link to code/data (score toward 10) versus only a conditional future promise to release it later or no mention at all (score toward 0). Score only which of these two patterns appears, not whether the code is actually good.
proposals.upstream_parent: author or lab pre-submission practice and venue norms around open-sourcing
proposals.rationale: R01 and R06 give live anonymized links (anonymous.4open.science), while R41 and R42 explicitly say code 'will be made publicly available' or 'open-sourced upon acceptance' -- a conditional promise; greater pre-submission engineering polish could be mixed with actual quality.

proposals.name: Placeholder or anonymization residue as a rush marker
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text contains an obviously unfinished placeholder or generic anonymization stand-in (e.g., a literal '<placeholder>' token, or the bare word 'anonymized' standing in for a real link) rather than a fully filled-in, specific reference. Score only the presence of such unfinished placeholders, not the overall polish of the writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing or rush at the moment the item was finalized for submission
proposals.rationale: R18 contains the literal token '$<$placeholder$>$' in place of its code link and R21 says 'Our code is available at anonymized' rather than an actual link, both readable signs the item was finished without a final proofreading pass.

proposals.name: Density of named-competitor differentiation within a narrow niche
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the abstract explicitly distinguishes its approach from three or more distinctly named prior variants or competing methods within the same narrow niche (score high) versus introducing a problem or benchmark with little or no differentiation from named prior competing approaches (score low). Score only the count and density of named-competitor differentiation, not whether the differentiation is convincing.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream -- how late the item arrives relative to other entries tackling adjacent problems
proposals.rationale: R55 differentiates itself from 'CLIP', 'CLIP's variants', and 'DINO' by name, and R17 differentiates from multiple named 'decoder refinement variants' and the specific 'HLR' baseline, reading as later, more crowded-conversation entries; by contrast R16 and R26 introduce new datasets/benchmarks with comparatively little named-competitor differentiation, reading as earlier entries in their niches.

proposals.name: Rhetorical framing as correcting a stated prior consensus
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the abstract explicitly frames its finding as overturning, contradicting, or correcting a stated prior belief or existing body of work (e.g., 'Contrary to previous findings...', 'we find that existing X are insufficient or cannot achieve...') versus simply presenting a new contribution without this contrastive framing. Score only the presence of this contrarian framing device, not whether the correction is actually justified.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream -- arriving after enough prior attempts exist to be contradicted
proposals.rationale: R18 opens with 'Contrary to previous findings, we show...' and R25 states 'all the representative prior works cannot achieve any system-level effect', both explicitly positioning themselves against a body of predecessor claims, a framing less available to an item among the first entries on its topic, such as R04's 'early training results' framing.

proposals.name: First-person process narration vs. results-first framing
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much of the abstract is phrased as first-person narration of the research process itself ('we study', 'we investigate', 'we examine', 'we explore how...') as opposed to leading with the artifact or result ('We propose X, which achieves Y%'). Score the ratio of process-narration phrasing to result-first phrasing; do not judge which style makes for better research.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('we examine how these two types of learning signals interact...') and R26 ('we hope to advance...we present HIVEX') both foreground open-ended process narration rather than a named artifact's headline number, unlike R01 or R15, which lead quickly into a named method and its quantitative outperformance.

proposals.name: Submission-cohort era markers in models, benchmarks and vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract's named models, benchmarks, datasets, metrics and terminology place the text in an older machine-learning era rather than the current one. 0 = the vocabulary is entirely contemporary (e.g. multimodal LLMs, agents, diffusion personalisation, LLM-as-evaluator); 10 = the vocabulary is entirely of an earlier era (e.g. CIFAR-10 top-1 error, MNIST/Reuters clustering, BLEU on WMT/IWSLT, BERT/RoBERTa probing, pointer networks, value-iteration networks). Count only era-identifying tokens: model names, benchmark names, metric names, hardware/time budgets, and stock phrases of a period. Do NOT judge whether older or newer topics are better, more important, or more rigorous; you are only measuring how strongly the text is time-stamped toward the older pole.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission year / cohort of the batch the item was drawn from
proposals.rationale: The slice's era distribution is lopsided: R04 (CIFAR-10 3.6% top-1, 36h search), R16 (BERT zero-shot fact completion, WebQuestions/Quasar-T), R31 (IWSLT 2014 and WMT 2018 BLEU records), R43 (value iteration networks, Curiosity rover) and R51 (SpectralNet on MNIST/Reuters) all sit on the dense_high_card_low side, while contemporary-vocabulary items such as R26 (MLLM benchmark curation) and R36 (LLM agent experience sharing) sit on the dense_low_card_high side. Vintage is a property of when the text was written, not of how good the work is, and a text-only model can read it off the vocabulary alone; it is mixed because field-wide standards for evidence also shift across cohorts.

proposals.name: Artifact-availability statement: anonymous link or promised release
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract contains explicit code/data availability language, counting both live anonymised artifact URLs and future-tense promises. Score higher when such language is present, prominent (its own closing sentence), specific (a full anonymised repository URL), or repeated for multiple artifacts; score 0 when no availability statement of any kind appears. Placeholder or redacted forms ('code available at <placeholder>', 'available at anonymized') count as present. Do NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, whether the promise is credible, or whether the artifact sounds valuable; measure only how much availability language is on the page.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice with the review-cycle's anonymisation tooling and release conventions
proposals.rationale: Availability boilerplate is concentrated on one side of the disagreement: R06, R07, R09, R26, R36, R41 and R49 all close with an anonymous.4open.science URL, R05 closes with '$<$placeholder$>$' and R25 with 'available at anonymized', while R02, R44 and R46 use the promissory form 'upon acceptance/publication' - nearly all dense_low_card_high. It is a boilerplate habit shaped by tooling and venue norms rather than a property of the research, and an explicitly checkable string is exactly what a criterion bank can reward. Tagged mixed because genuine reproducibility discipline plausibly co-causes both the string and real quality.

proposals.name: Density of quantified deltas and headline numbers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract is populated with concrete numbers: percentages, absolute scores, multiplicative factors, speedups, error values, parameter or sample counts, and explicit before/after comparisons against a named prior number. 0 = no quantities at all, the contribution is described only in words; 10 = numbers appear in most sentences of the results portion, including at least one explicit 'X to Y' or 'ours N vs. baseline M' contrast. Count occurrences and their spread across sentences. Do NOT assess whether the numbers are impressive, plausible, well-controlled, or fairly compared, and do not penalise or reward the absence of numbers as a sign of rigour; count only how much numeric material is present.
proposals.rationale: Numeric saturation tracks the split: R06 (MAE 1.897e-3 vs 27.074e-3), R30 (67.39% vs 58.90% AUC-ROC), R41 (335.5 fps), R44 (38.9% to 44.3% to 45.5%, 5x), R53 (75% vs 68% at eps=2) and R05 (81.88-88.81%) are dense_low_card_high, whereas number-free or number-sparse items R08, R17, R57 and R58 are all dense_high_card_low. A fixed criterion bank can literally count digits, so numeric density is the kind of feature a scorecard over-rewards; it is not itself quality (the same delta can be cherry-picked or trivially obtained), though it is tagged mixed because real evidence often does arrive as numbers.

proposals.name: Acronym and coined-component proliferation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT of acronym and coined-name machinery in the abstract: a branded system name, plus named sub-modules, sub-methods, stages or phases each given their own capitalised abbreviation, plus field acronyms used as shorthand. 0 = no coined names or abbreviations at all; 10 = a top-level branded acronym plus two or more nested component acronyms plus several field abbreviations, so that most sentences carry at least one capitalised short form. Count distinct abbreviations and how often they recur. Do NOT judge whether the naming is apt, memorable, clear or clunky, and do not treat a modular decomposition as evidence of a well-structured method; count only how much naming machinery is on the page.
proposals.rationale: Nested-acronym texts cluster on the dense_low_card_high side: R46 stacks IKL over IUR and ICL, R09 stacks GenSE over SE plus semantic/acoustic token stages, R47 stacks MoBSE over sEEG and VAD, R50 gives GCReinSL over SL/RL/TD, and R41 gives PAR-AdvGAN over AdvGAN. Coining a named sub-module for each paragraph makes a method look enumerable and component-complete to a checklist without adding anything to the underlying contribution, which is why it is predictive here but is a naming habit rather than quality.

proposals.name: Markup residue and layout damage from the paste path
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT of raw source residue and layout damage visible in the abstract text: unrendered LaTeX commands (\textit, \emph, \textsf, \url, \footnote, escaped \% or \times), stray math delimiters around ordinary words, markdown asterisks used for emphasis, mid-word hyphen breaks left over from PDF column wrapping, hard line breaks in the middle of sentences, doubled spaces, and blank-line paragraph splits inside a single abstract. 0 = clean rendered prose with no residue; 10 = residue of several distinct kinds appearing repeatedly. Do NOT treat residue as sloppiness or cleanliness as care, and do not judge the writing at all; count only the visible artifacts.
proposals.upstream_parent: the copy-paste / text-extraction path used to enter the abstract (LaTeX source vs. PDF vs. plain textarea)
proposals.rationale: Residue is common in this slice and is orthogonal to content: R05 shows '$<$placeholder$>$', R07 carries \textsf around individual letters, R13 has '\textit{e.g.,}', R44 an unrendered \footnote, R49 a bare \url, R53 \emph, R37 markdown bold asterisks, while R11 shows PDF-column hyphen breaks ('chal-lenging') and R10 hard mid-sentence wraps. Which artifact appears is determined by where the author copied the text from, a fact about tooling that leaves a strong textual fingerprint while carrying no information about the research.

proposals.name: Field-importance preamble before the contribution appears
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract opens with general field-importance or textbook-background material before naming its own contribution. Measure how much of the opening is spent asserting that the area matters, defining standard terms, or narrating the field's history, and how late the first 'we propose / we introduce / this paper presents' arrives. 0 = the very first sentence states the contribution; 10 = three or more sentences of scene-setting and definition precede any mention of what the authors did. Do NOT judge whether the framing is well-motivated, whether the background is accurate, or whether directness is better writing; measure only the amount of pre-contribution material.
proposals.upstream_parent: the writing school / venue habitus in which the author was trained (thesis-style vs. contribution-first conventions)
proposals.rationale: The two openings split the slice: long field-importance preambles appear in R02 ('Deep learning is slowly, but steadily, hitting a memory bottleneck'), R06 ('Numerical interpolation for scattered data ... is widely used'), R40 ('Faces and humans are crucial elements in social interaction') and R20 ('Games have been vital test beds'), all dense_low_card_high, whereas contribution-first openings in R18 ('This paper introduces Meta-Q-Learning'), R28, R54 and R60 are all dense_high_card_low. Rhetorical ordering is a convention absorbed from one's training environment, not a property of the result, though the same environment plausibly also shapes genuine quality.

proposals.name: Ornate register with minor agreement and idiom slips
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the prose combines elevated, thesaurus-reaching vocabulary with small idiomatic or agreement irregularities. Look for both together: ornate substitutions where a plain word would do ('purposive assembly', 'in an endeavor to enhance the efficacy', 'endeavors to reduce', 'commendable results', 'fluidly combine'), and local slips such as subject-verb disagreement, dropped or doubled articles, odd prepositions, or a misspelling. 0 = plain, idiomatic, slip-free prose; 10 = ornate diction throughout with several visible slips. Do NOT judge whether the writing is good, clear, or professional, and do not infer anything about the author; score only how much of this register-plus-slip texture is present in the text.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's first language and the amount of copy-editing or writing assistance available to them
proposals.rationale: This texture is concentrated on the dense_low_card_high side: R01 ('purposive assembly of LoRA modules', 'excluding the necessity of in-context examples'), R44 ('In an endeavor to enhance the efficacy'), R46 ('endeavors to reduce the bias'), R50 ('yielding commendable results'), plus outright slips in R35 ('obstrusive') and R12 ('This thus inevitably raise a critical research question'). Language background is not quality, and this is the textual trace it leaves; tagged mixed because access to copy-editing tracks lab resources, which plausibly also raise genuine quality.

proposals.name: Frontier-compute and proprietary-model access fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract's experiments imply access to large-scale or non-public training infrastructure. Raise the score for: pretraining or modifying an industry-scale proprietary model rather than using a public checkpoint off the shelf; reporting full pretraining runs, FLOP budgets, or wall-clock savings on such runs; competing on large-scale production benchmarks; and casual use of internal model names as if they were commonly available. Lower it for experiments describable on commodity hardware or on public checkpoints at inference only. Do NOT judge whether the scale is warranted, whether the results are strong, or whether large-scale work is more valuable; measure only how strongly the text implies large-scale infrastructure.
proposals.rationale: The industrial-scale fingerprint is one-sided here: R48 modifies PaLM's pretraining objective and reports SuperGLUE 55.7 to 59.2, R15 pretrains BERT and UL2 with 20-33% FLOP savings against gradual stacking, R42 injects knowledge into BERT/RoBERTa, and R31 sets WMT/IWSLT BLEU records - all dense_high_card_low. Who can afford the experiment is an unseen factor, but it leaves an unmistakable trace in which models and budgets are named. Tagged mixed because resources genuinely buy more convincing experiments as well as prestige.

proposals.name: Topic crowding: bandwagon proximity versus off-stream subject
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract's subject sits inside the currently most crowded region of submissions rather than off to one side. 10 = the topic and framing are squarely in the densest current stream (large or multimodal language models, prompting, agents, LLM evaluation and benchmarks, diffusion personalisation, jailbreaks and alignment); 0 = the topic sits well outside it (classical statistics or optimisation, non-ML application domains, cognitive-science-inspired studies, robotics for specialised platforms, signal processing). Judge from topic nouns, benchmark names and the community the framing addresses. Do NOT judge whether the topic is important, timely, overcrowded, or worth pursuing; measure only its distance from the crowded centre.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the item's topic in the stream of entries (how crowded the container is around it)
proposals.rationale: Off-stream subjects are heavily represented among dense_high_card_low: R59 (decision diagrams and spatial branch-and-cut for norm constraints), R52 (infant visual learning and feature alignment), R43 (planetary rover navigation), R58 (non-stationary Hawkes kernels) and R28 (quasi-Newton meta-learned inverse Hessians), while crowded-centre items such as R26, R36, R40 and R14 sit on the dense_low_card_high side. Crowding is a property of the container, not the work; it leaves a trace only through topic vocabulary, which is what the judge scores. Mixed because hot areas also attract concentrations of strong authors.

proposals.name: Late-entrant riff: narrow delta on a named recent predecessor
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the abstract defines itself as an increment on one specifically named prior method rather than as a fresh reading of a problem. Raise the score when the text names a particular predecessor method or paper (including inline citations such as 'Author et al., year'), states that it extends, repairs, generalises or ablates that specific thing, and states its contribution as the delta against it; lower it when the problem is posed from scratch and prior work is referenced only as an undifferentiated 'existing approaches'. Do NOT judge whether incremental or from-scratch work is better, whether the delta is significant, or whether the predecessor was well chosen; measure only how tightly the contribution is bound to a named predecessor.
proposals.upstream_parent: position and timing of the entry in the submission stream (writing after the obvious takes are already claimed)
proposals.rationale: Mode-3 fingerprint: an item written late in a crowded stream must differentiate against takes already claimed, and that shows up as a named-predecessor delta. R13 is explicitly an extension of 'the effective hybrid latent refinement (HLR) method' with a distribution-regularisation patch, R41 is 'Progressive Auto-Regression AdvGAN' positioned against the original AdvGAN, R15 measures itself against gradual stacking with an inline '(Reddi et al., 2023)', and R08 builds on 'prover-verifier games (Anil et al., 2021)' - none of which tells you whether the work is good. Inline citation of a specific lineage is itself an insider practice trace. Tagged mixed because a late entrant who has read the obvious takes may also produce genuinely sharper work.

proposals.name: Canonical abstract template
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text follows a recognizable problem-gap-method-results-conclusion sequence with explicit signposting. Judge only extent of this structure; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: practiced abstract-writing conventions leave this textual fingerprint, which can affect reception independently of substance and may also accompany real competence. Visible examples include R04, R31, and R56.

proposals.name: Promotional intensifiers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the presence of promotional intensifiers such as novel, significant, comprehensive, superior, robust, impressive, or first. Judge only extent of the wording; do not judge whether the claims are good or true.
proposals.rationale: This is a stylistic rhetoric cue rather than a property of the method. It appears prominently in R03, R17, and R35.

proposals.name: Acronym branding density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract introduces acronyms, stylized names, expansions, or branded method labels. Judge only naming density; do not judge whether the names are good.
proposals.rationale: Memorable labels can attract attention through presentation alone, without indicating substance. Examples include R07, R22, and R40.

proposals.name: Numerical result ornamentation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the density of exact numbers, percentages, decimal metrics, speedups, dataset counts, and baseline margins. Judge only visible numerical detail; do not judge whether the results are good.
proposals.rationale: Precise-looking quantities can function as persuasive surface signals regardless of their evidential meaning. This fingerprint is visible in R20, R23, and R59.

proposals.name: Availability signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for explicit code, data, demo, repository, or open-source availability statements and links. Judge only extent of availability signaling; do not judge whether the resources are good or usable.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: venue-aware authors may add standardized resource language that affects reception; the same practice can also support genuine reproducibility. Examples include R07, R22, and R40.

proposals.name: Formal guarantee cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for visible formalism such as theorem references, proofs, convergence claims, bounds, regret rates, complexity statements, or mathematical notation. Judge only extent of these cues; do not judge correctness or quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: communities and authors differ in how much formal assurance they foreground. This can influence impressions and may also correlate with actual rigor. Examples include R18, R38, and R57.

proposals.name: Application-scope sprawl
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how extensively the abstract lists multiple domains, tasks, modalities, datasets, languages, or use cases. Judge only breadth of listed scope; do not judge whether the breadth is good.
proposals.rationale: Topic breadth is a visible scope cue that can create an impression of generality without itself being quality. Examples include R03, R14, and R40.

proposals.name: Late-entry differentiation language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text enumerates prior approaches, their limitations, and explicit distinctions establishing why this contribution is different. Judge only extent of differentiation language; do not judge whether the distinction is good.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and position in the entry stream
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: a later entrant in a crowded stream may leave a fingerprint of extensive boundary-setting; additional revision time may also affect genuine substance. Examples include R08, R16, and R49.

proposals.name: Generic prompt uptake
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much broad, generic field motivation precedes the concrete technical object, contribution, or experiment. Judge only the amount and placement of generic framing; do not judge whether the framing is good.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: an early or obvious response to a prompt may reuse broad framing before differentiation is needed. This positional fingerprint appears in R14, R15, and R60.

proposals.name: Prestige-anchor references
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract foregrounds famous models, benchmarks, datasets, institutions, or record comparisons as reference points. Judge only extent of prestige anchoring; do not judge whether the references are good.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: anticipated audience familiarity can encourage recognizable names and headline comparisons, creating a social-attention cue independent of substance. Examples include R03, R29, and R47.

proposals.name: Length and discourse density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of long multi-paragraph structure, numerous clauses, and elaborated transitions; do not judge whether the feature is good or indicative of quality.
proposals.rationale: Formatting stamina and verbosity can become proxies for author familiarity or submission conventions without measuring contribution quality. The pattern is visible in the extended, multi-paragraph presentations in R01 and R22.

proposals.name: Acronym and coined-name density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent to which the abstract introduces multiple acronyms, capitalized method names, or branded component names; do not judge whether the names are useful or the method is good.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in naming methods and field conventions
proposals.rationale: Naming conventions can reveal disciplinary style and author practice, while also attracting attention independently of substance. Examples include the clusters of names in R05 and R29.

proposals.name: Quantitative result saturation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of numerical metrics, percentage changes, dataset counts, speed figures, and baseline comparisons; do not judge whether the numbers are impressive, credible, or indicative of quality.
proposals.rationale: A results-heavy presentation may proxy for field norms, laboratory resources, or familiarity with benchmark reporting rather than quality itself. This fingerprint is prominent in R08 and R13.

proposals.name: Priority-claim rhetoric
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of phrases claiming novelty, being first, setting records, superiority, or state-of-the-art status; do not judge whether any claim is true or good.
proposals.rationale: Superlative and priority language can influence textual impressions through rhetoric alone, without establishing scientific merit. Such wording appears in R12 and R42.

proposals.name: Artifact-availability signaling
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent to which the abstract advertises code, data, demos, repositories, or future public release; do not judge whether the artifacts are complete, useful, or good.
proposals.rationale: Artifact signaling can proxy for venue familiarity, compliance habits, or lab infrastructure, while artifact-producing practice may also correlate with genuine quality. Examples occur in R05 and R18.

proposals.name: Citation-lineage anchoring
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of explicit references to named models, benchmark families, datasets, prior baselines, or established research lineages; do not judge whether the lineage is appropriate or the work is good.
proposals.upstream_parent: community embeddedness and field-specific writing practice
proposals.rationale: Dense lineage anchoring can expose disciplinary membership and familiarity with expected reference points, independently of contribution quality. The fingerprint is clear in R02 and R49.

proposals.name: Urgency and impact framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of language invoking safety, security, clinical importance, societal urgency, ecological challenges, or broad real-world impact; do not judge whether the issue is important or the claims are justified.
proposals.rationale: High-stakes framing can attract attention through audience values and topical salience without measuring the technical contribution. It is visible in R12 and R60.

proposals.name: Formula and notation density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of mathematical symbols, equations, asymptotic notation, specialized variables, and LaTeX-style expressions; do not judge whether the mathematics is correct, rigorous, or good.
proposals.rationale: Notation density can act as a typography or disciplinary-style proxy that affects readability and model perception without being quality. Examples include R35 and R59.

proposals.name: Late-riff textual fingerprint
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent to which the abstract contrasts several established approaches, layers together recent ingredients, and frames the method as a response to an already crowded line of work; do not infer actual submission order or judge whether the synthesis is good.
proposals.rationale: A late-stream entrant may textually reflect awareness of obvious prior takes and produce a contrastive synthesis; this is a position proxy, though such awareness can also support genuine quality. The fingerprint appears in R03 and R32.

proposals.name: Trend-buzzword saturation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of currently fashionable technical labels and application terms, such as LLM, foundation model, generative AI, alignment, prompting, or multimodal; do not judge whether the topic is timely, important, or good.
proposals.rationale: Fashionable terminology can proxy for attention cycles, community momentum, and audience familiarity rather than intrinsic quality; those same ecosystems may also provide better tools or collaborators. Examples include R21 and R31.

proposals.name: Abstract length and verbosity
proposals.instruction: Estimate raw verbosity: word count and sentence density. 0 = very short or sparse abstract; 10 = among the longest and most wordy. This is an extent-of-volume item only; do not treat longer or shorter as better or worse.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's editing and packing practice in the abstract format
proposals.rationale: Verbosity gives more text for a checklist-style reader to map onto criteria without being substance. The slice includes long, packed entries such as R02 and R17, and leaner entries such as R32 and R58; length can separate them independently of idea quality.

proposals.name: Formulaic problem-gap-solution template
proposals.instruction: How completely does the abstract follow the canonical machine-learning recipe: background, however/challenge gap, in-this-paper-we-propose statement, method summary, and experimental-results sentence? 0 = no canonical moves; 10 = all moves present and densely formulaic. Score template presence, never whether the template is good.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice with conference abstract conventions
proposals.rationale: Template completeness can be read as coverage even when it is boilerplate. R05, R14, and R26 move through nearly every slot, while R28 and R46 frame ideas in a less slot-driven way.

proposals.name: Typographic and markup emphasis density
proposals.instruction: How much non-plain emphasis or markup appears: bold, markdown bold or italics, LaTeX-style emphasis, bold, italics, sans-serif, URL commands, math tokens, and uppercase styled acronyms? 0 = plain prose; 10 = pervasive markup. Do not judge whether emphasis improves readability.
proposals.rationale: Markup can draw attention to named contributions and metrics without adding quality. R05 bolds COMM, R02 uses emphasis, R10 and R26 use italics, and R27 uses styled system letters; R31 and R32 are plainer.

proposals.name: Branded method or system acronym spotlighting
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract create and repeat a branded method, system, dataset, or acronym name, such as LoraHub, COMM, MONeT, SAFARI, or CerebroVoice? 0 = no branded name; 10 = a brand introduced early and repeated as the anchor. Score branding extent, not whether the name is clever or valuable.
proposals.rationale: A memorable brand can look like a concrete contribution apart from substance. R01, R27, R40, and R56 foreground branded names, while R22, R28, and R31 do not lean on naming.

proposals.name: Quantitative result and metric dump density
proposals.instruction: How dense are explicit numerical performance claims: percentages, accuracy, BLEU or F1 numbers, speedups, and before/after metric contrasts? 0 = none; 10 = many numbers and comparative metrics. Score density only; do not assess whether the results are strong, valid, or important.
proposals.rationale: Metric dumps can satisfy an evidence criterion without being quality, and may reflect compute or lab resources. R02, R39, and R41 are number-heavy, while R22, R28, and R46 give little or no metric dump.

proposals.name: Code, data, and resource-release signaling
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract mention released artifacts: URLs, anonymous repositories, code/data available, release upon acceptance, datasets, or benchmarks? 0 = none; 10 = release language is prominent or repeated. Do not score whether release is useful or high quality.
proposals.rationale: Availability signaling can impress a criterion-based reader separately from the core idea. R14, R18, R27, R50, and R56 include release statements, while R03, R24, and R31 do not.

proposals.name: Named high-resource model and benchmark references
proposals.instruction: How often does the text invoke well-known large models, datasets, benchmarks, or leaderboards, such as GPT-4o, PaLM, ImageNet, CIFAR, WMT, Big-Bench, or LibriSpeech? 0 = none; 10 = many such named resources. Count references; do not judge relevance or quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional resources, seniority, and community network
proposals.rationale: Familiar infrastructure names may act as credibility markers unrelated to the contribution. R01 cites Big-Bench, R08 lists GPT-4o and related systems, R39 cites WMT records, and R57 cites LibriSpeech; R28 and R47 use fewer recognizable infrastructure names.

proposals.name: AI-assisted or promotional boilerplate register
proposals.instruction: How much promotional or generic abstract phrasing occurs, such as paving the way, shedding light, immense capabilities, crucial, vital, innovative, unlock, or whistleblower? 0 = absent; 10 = heavy promotional register. Score wording only; do not judge whether the framing is persuasive or good.
proposals.rationale: Fluent promotional boilerplate can be mistaken for polish. R15, R17, R20, and R29 contain such phrases, while R24, R31, and R46 use a more neutral technical register.

proposals.name: Negative gap-framing density
proposals.instruction: How much does the text inflate a problem or gap using however, unfortunately, limited, lack, remains underexplored, critical, challenging, or cannot? 0 = no gap-framing; 10 = constant negative framing. Score frequency and intensity, not whether the gap is real.
proposals.rationale: Gap language can make an abstract appear motivated without adding quality. R02, R05, R10, R14, and R50 foreground limitations, while R28, R31, and R47 use less inflated gap framing.

proposals.name: Late-stream meta or saturation entry tell
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract read as a late-arriving entry in a crowded stream: proposing a benchmark or meta-evaluation, compressing or pruning existing benchmarks, claiming a first after many prior works, or framing the area as saturated or redundant? 0 = no late-stream positioning tells; 10 = pervasive late-stream or meta positioning. Score textual tells only; do not judge whether being late or meta is good. The judge cannot see the actual submission order.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry and research stream
proposals.rationale: Late-stream positioning can look timely from criteria but is not itself quality. R37 and R50 explicitly compress or repair saturated evaluation, R34 and R08 present new comprehensive benchmarks after existing options, while R28 reads more like a foundational framing.
